claims_about_writeup.quote: experiments/steer_jlens/method.md — the 294-word doc for your method section
claims_about_writeup.why: method.md is indeed a short, dense write-up of the method intended for a method section; a manual word count comes out close to the low-300s range, consistent with the claimed ~294 words.
method.md's final line explicitly lists these same three vector files as the vectors beside the file.

message_source_quote: Your paper says the right readout is `J_l(h_l − μ_l)`. Flip the sign and that becomes a steering vector
writeup_source_quote: The paper's Taylor reading J(h − μ) ≈ f(h) − f(μ) makes the released lens (μ = 0) an expansion about an off-data point, and the μ ladder picks the best counterfactual: a matched reference mean. Sign-flipped, this is a steering method

differences.what: Novelty/differentiation from other steering methods (CAA/attitude vectors) and a cross-reference to Herrera's draft showing those don't affect recall
differences.message_quote: It's not a reproduction of any existing method: CAA/attitude vectors steer *behavioural* contrasts (and Herrera's draft shows those don't touch recall); this vector *is* the paper's μ, derived from the Taylor reading `J(h−μ) ≈ f(h) − f(μ)`.

rationale: Both documents treat the source the same way: they name it only as 'the paper'/'your paper' (an unmistakable pointer to Raman 2026, since no other prior work is referenced) and both say the steering method is obtained by sign-flipping the paper's centred readout J(h−μ), i.e. credits-level attribution and overlap in both. The message additionally stakes a stronger, more explicit novelty claim — contrasting the method with CAA/attitude-vector steering and citing Herrera's draft as evidence those don't touch recall — which the write-up's method.md does not mention at all, making the message's novelty framing slightly richer/more elaborated than the write-up's.
